Short answer: the bike didn't get faster, the conditions did. First principles, this is almost entirely aerodynamics plus psychology.

The dominant factor is drafting. When you ride in a pack, you sit in the low-pressure pocket behind the rider ahead, and that cuts your aerodynamic drag by roughly 20 to 40 percent depending on how tight the line is. Drag is the single biggest force fighting you above about 15 mph, so removing a third of it at the same pedal effort means you go noticeably faster (or the same speed for less work). That is the "the bike is flying today" feeling, and it is real, it is just your slipstream, not your frame.

Then the human layer. Group rides pull a harder effort out of you than solo rides: you surge out of corners to close gaps, you hold a wheel you would have let go alone, your cadence climbs to match the pack. You are simply putting more watts down, and the bike reports that as performance.

So the ranking: draft effect first (biggest), group effort second, recent drivetrain refresh third. Nothing is wrong with the bike (and nothing is wrong with you) for noticing it feels better with company. It genuinely does.

If you want to prove it to yourself: ride the same loop solo and with the group, same route, same day, and compare average power against average speed on your Garmin. If your speed goes up while your power stays flat, that delta is the draft. That is the experiment, go run it.

**Brown before you seal.** The cooker can't brown, full stop. Anything with fat or protein (beef, pork shoulder, chicken thighs) goes in a hot pan first. That crust is where the flavor is. Skip it and everything tastes flat and steamed.
